questions.stem: Under Rule 2(a), who is not excused from the consequences of neglecting to comply with the Rules?
options: Only the person at the helm at the time
Only the master, as the person in command
The vessel, owner, master and crew
Only the owner, since the owner controls the vessel
questions.explanation: Rule 2(a) names the vessel, the owner, the master and the crew. Responsibility is not limited to whoever was steering.

questions.stem: Besides the written Rules, what else can require a vessel to take a precaution under Rule 2(a)?
options: Ordinary practice of seamen, or special circumstances
The wishes of the vessel's owner or charterer
The instructions of the other vessel's master
The company's insurance conditions
questions.explanation: Rule 2(a) refers to precautions required by the ordinary practice of seamen or by the special circumstances of the case. Owner wishes, another vessel's instructions and insurance terms are not what the Rule names.

questions.stem: Rule 2(b) allows a departure from the Rules in certain circumstances. Which statement best describes when this is justified?
options: Whenever following the Rules would cost extra time or fuel
To avoid immediate danger, weighing all special circumstances
Whenever the other vessel is smaller than your own
Whenever the master judges that the Rules are out of date
questions.explanation: Departure is justified only when it is necessary to avoid immediate danger, and only after giving due regard to the dangers of navigation and collision and the special circumstances, including the vessels' limitations. Convenience, relative size or a personal view about the Rules do not qualify.

questions.stem: You are the stand-on vessel in a crossing situation. The give-way vessel has not acted and you see you could clear her safely by turning early, well before any danger is immediate. You decide to hold on because "it is her duty to keep clear." What is the main problem with this thinking?
options: None, because the stand-on vessel never needs to do anything
Rule 2(a): neglecting a precaution leaves you answerable
Rule 2(b) forbids the stand-on vessel from ever changing course
Holding on is only allowed if the other vessel has radar
questions.explanation: Rule 2(a) keeps responsibility on the vessel, owner, master and crew for neglecting precautions required by ordinary seamanship or the circumstances. The other vessel's fault is not a complete defence. Later Rules set out exactly when and how the stand-on vessel may act, which you will study separately.

questions.stem: A master says, "Rule 2 means I can set aside any Rule I think is awkward, as long as I record my reasons in the log." Which response is most accurate?
options: Correct, if logged within 1 h
Incorrect: 2(b) covers only avoiding immediate danger
Correct, because Rule 2(a) gives masters full discretion
Incorrect, because Rule 2 never allows any departure from the Rules
questions.explanation: Rule 2(b) does allow departure, but only where it is needed to avoid immediate danger and after due regard to the dangers and special circumstances. A log entry does not widen that. The last option is wrong because Rule 2(b) does recognise justified departures.

questions.stem: Close to a tug with a long tow, you decide that the normal action under the Rules would lead into immediate danger and you must do something different. Under Rule 2(b), what must you take into account when choosing your action?
options: Only your own vessel's speed, since the other vessel is not your concern
All dangers and special circumstances, incl. both vessels' limits
Nothing further, because once danger is immediate any action is acceptable
Only what the company's operating manual says to do
questions.explanation: Rule 2(b) requires due regard to all dangers of navigation and collision and to special circumstances, including the limitations of the vessels involved. A tug and long tow may be unable to stop or turn quickly, so an action that relies on her manoeuvring could make things worse. Immediate danger justifies departing from the Rules, but it does not remove the need to judge the whole situation.
